config.title: Reverse Linked List

intro.title: Reverse Linked List
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that reverses a singly linked list. You will learn the core concept of pointer manipulation by iteratively changing the direction of the links between nodes. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, while loops, and basic object references to represent nodes. This hands-on exercise will help you understand how to traverse and modify data structures efficiently.
intro.usecase: Reversing linked lists is essential in UI components that manage ordered data, such as undo/redo stacks in text editors or document processors. It's also used in navigation systems where you need to reverse a route or in social media feeds that allow users to toggle between chronological and reverse-chronological display. Understanding this algorithm helps developers implement features like browser history traversal, playlist reversal in media players, or reordering task lists in productivity apps.

objectives: Construct a linked list data structure using JavaScript classes
Initialize a linked list with multiple nodes for testing reversal
Manipulate node pointers to reverse the direction of a linked list
Implement an iterative algorithm to reverse a linked list
Apply pointer reassignment logic to traverse and modify the list
Control the reversal process by managing previous, current, and next pointers
Integrate the reversal function into a complete working program

content.body: Have you ever tried reading a sentence backwards, one word at a time? That's what we'll do with a linked list! We'll learn how to reverse the order of nodes so the last becomes first and the first becomes last.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain why we can't use indexes to jump around in a linked list
• Implement a pointer-based approach to reverse a linked list
• Walk through the reversal process node by node
• Keep track of the head pointer to avoid losing nodes
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you have a chain of 3 nodes: A → B → C → null. How would you reverse it to C → B → A → null? Think about how you'd move through the chain one node at a time.
content.title: Try it

content.body: Start at node A. You can only see A's value and that it points to B. You can't jump directly to C. How would you get from A to B to C? What information would you need to remember as you move?
content.title: Walk it through

content.body: When you're at node B, you know it points to C. To reverse the list, you need to make B point to A instead. But if you change B's pointer, you lose the connection to C! How can you avoid losing nodes?
content.title: Think about connections

content.body: You just walked through the list node by node, thinking about how to change pointers without losing connections. This is the core challenge of linked list manipulation!
content.title: What you did

content.body: With 3 nodes, you can keep track in your head. But what about 100 nodes? You need a systematic way to reverse pointers while moving forward. Can't figure it out? Let's explore the approach together.
content.title: Why it gets tricky

content.body: In arrays, we can jump to any position with an index. But in linked lists, we can only move to the next node (or previous if doubly linked). We need to use pointers to remember where we are, where we came from, and where we're going next.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like turning a chain of paper clips around. You can only hold one clip at a time, and you need to carefully reconnect each one to the previous clip as you go.

content.body: We'll use three pointers: current (where we are), previous (where we came from), and next (where we're going). As we move through the list, we'll reverse the current node's pointer to point to previous, then move all pointers forward one step.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start with previous = null, current = head
2. While current is not null:
   a. Store next node (current.next)
   b. Reverse current's pointer to point to previous
   c. Move previous to current
   d. Move current to next
3. Return previous (new head)
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up pointers
steps.instruction: Initialize the three pointers we need: previous, current, and next. Start with previous as null and current as the head of the list.
steps.hint: Remember: previous starts as null because the first node will become the last node, which should point to null.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that declares previous and current variables with initial values
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Don't forget to initialize previous as null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need two variables: previous (null) and current (head).

steps.title: Start the loop
steps.instruction: Create a while loop that continues as long as current is not null. We need to process each node in the list.
steps.hint: The loop should run while we still have nodes to process.
steps.expectedOutcome: A while loop with the correct condition
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Check your condition - we want to continue while current exists.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need a while loop that runs while current is not null.

steps.title: Save the next node
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, store current.next in a variable called next before we change it. This prevents us from losing the connection to the rest of the list.
steps.hint: We need to save the next node reference before we modify current.next.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that stores current.next in a next variable
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure you're storing current.next, not just declaring a variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to save current.next to a variable called next.

steps.title: Reverse the pointer
steps.instruction: Now reverse the current node's pointer. Make current.next point to previous instead of next.
steps.hint: This is where we actually change the direction of the arrow.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that sets current.next to previous
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've turned the node around to point backward.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. We need to change current.next to point to previous.
steps.feedbackWrong: We should set current.next = previous to reverse the pointer.

steps.title: Move pointers forward
steps.instruction: After reversing the pointer, move previous to current and current to next. This advances our position in the list.
steps.hint: We need to update both pointers to continue to the next node.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that updates previous and current
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You're walking through the list one step at a time.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Don't forget to update both previous and current.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need: previous = current; current = next;

steps.title: Return the new head
steps.instruction: After the loop finishes, previous will be pointing to the new head of the reversed list. Return previous.
steps.hint: When the loop ends, current is null and previous is the last node we processed, which is now the first node.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've completed the reversal algorithm.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Think about what variable holds the new head after the loop.
steps.feedbackWrong: We should return previous, which is the new head of the reversed list.

content.body: You've successfully implemented linked list reversal! Remember: in linked lists, we walk node by node using pointers. The key is to save the next node before changing pointers, and always keep track of where you came from (previous) and where you're going (next). This pointer dance is fundamental to many linked list algorithms.
